1.title: Two Names
1.context: Sosthenes shares the sender line. Acts 18:17 used the same name in this city, for the synagogue ruler beaten before Gallio's bench; the letter calls its co-sender brother and says no more, so the telling asserts nothing beyond both texts.
1.question: Who has stood beside your name on something that mattered, and what did their presence say?

1.title: Grace and Peace
1.context: The greeting is the standard opening of Paul's letters: grace first, then peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together.
1.question: What would change if you heard grace spoken over you before any correction?

1.title: Enriched in Every Way
1.context: The thanksgiving is specific: speech, knowledge, confirmed testimony, no gift lacking, and God's own keeping to the end. It stands in the letter just before the first rebuke.
1.question: What grace in your life do you thank God for least often because it feels normal?

1.title: No Divisions
1.context: The appeal names its source: Chloe's household. Paul does not hide where the report came from, and the report itself is never dramatized in the letter.
1.question: When you hear a hard report about people you love, what do you do with it first?

1.title: The Slogans
1.context: Four banners, four teachers, one of them Christ himself, used as a faction label. Apollos had watered what Paul planted in Corinth; Cephas is Peter.
1.question: Which teacher, church, or voice do you treat as your banner more than you admit?

1.title: Three Questions
1.context: The argument is made entirely of questions. A divided Christ, a crucified Paul, and a baptism in a man's name collapse the slogans without any added claim.
1.question: Which question in this verse presses hardest on your own loyalties?

1.title: Hardly Any Baptisms
1.context: Crispus was the synagogue ruler of Acts 18:8; Gaius and the household of Stephanas complete a deliberately short list. Paul's faulty memory here is a feature: no one can build a party on it.
1.question: What have you been relieved to have done less of, for the gospel's sake?

1.title: Not Sent to Baptize
1.context: The mission statement of the letter: preaching without wisdom-display, so the cross keeps its power. The next verse begins the argument about that cross.
1.question: Where are you tempted to compete with polish when the message itself is enough?

2.title: Foolishness and Power
2.context: The same message carries two verdicts depending on the hearer's direction: perishing or being saved. Both words describe a road in progress, not a final label.
2.question: Which verdict on the cross do the people closest to you mostly hold?

2.title: It Is Written
2.context: The quotation is Isaiah 29:14. Paul argues from Scripture before he argues from experience, and the questions that follow are addressed to the whole learned world.
2.question: What piece of human wisdom do you most need God to frustrate in your own thinking?

2.title: Through the Foolishness of What Was Preached
2.context: The world's wisdom had its opportunity and did not arrive at God. The rescue came by a preached message, the method Corinth's taste in speakers was busy despising.
2.question: How did the message first reach you, and who carried it?

2.title: Christ Crucified
2.context: Signs for one audience, wisdom for the other, and the preaching refuses both tests. To the called, the same Christ is both the power and the wisdom asked for.
2.question: What test do you quietly put to God before you will trust him?

2.title: Not Many Wise, Not Many Powerful
2.context: The congregation's own makeup is the evidence. God's choosing runs downhill by the world's scale: the foolish, the weak, the lowly, the things that are not.
2.question: Where has God met you in what the world counts as your weakness?

2.title: Boast in the Lord
2.context: Christ himself is named as the wisdom the Corinthians were seeking elsewhere, carrying righteousness, holiness, and redemption with him. The closing quotation is Jeremiah 9:24.
2.question: If all boasting moved to the Lord, what conversation in your life would change first?

3.title: Resolved to Know Nothing
3.context: The resolve was made before arrival: one subject, Jesus Christ and him crucified. Acts 18 records the long Corinth stay this preaching filled.
3.question: What have you resolved to keep at the center when everything else competes for it?

3.title: Weakness and Fear
3.context: Trembling is presented as strategy, not accident: faith that rests on God's power survives the speaker's absence, and Paul was about to be absent for years.
3.question: Where might your weakness be doing better work than your strength would?

3.title: A Message of Wisdom
3.context: The wisdom is real but redefined: mysterious, hidden, and destined before time began. The rulers of this age are already described as coming to nothing.
3.question: What do you treat as wisdom that is actually just the fashion of this age?

3.title: The Lord of Glory
3.context: Ignorance, not knowledge, crucified him: the rulers would not have done it had they understood. The written words of verse 9 weave Isaiah 64:4 with Jeremiah 3:16.
3.question: What have you done in ignorance that understanding would have prevented?

3.title: Revealed by the Spirit
3.context: Searches is an explorer's word: the Spirit goes into the deep things of God the way no outsider can. Revelation is the chapter's hinge from hidden to given.
3.question: What has God revealed to you slowly, over years, rather than all at once?

3.title: The Spirit Who Is From God
3.context: The argument runs from the human spirit's private knowledge to God's. The gift named here is understanding what God has freely given, a receipt noticed, not a prize earned.
3.question: What has God freely given you that you have not yet understood as a gift?

3.title: The Mind of Christ
3.context: The closing quotation is Isaiah 40:13. Paul applies it and then answers it with the claim the whole letter will test: we have the mind of Christ.
3.question: Where does your thinking least resemble the mind of Christ right now?

4.title: Infants in Christ
4.context: Milk and solid food measure growth by diet, and the evidence of infancy is relational: jealousy and dissension, not ignorance. The slogans are quoted back as the symptom.
4.question: What is your own most reliable sign that you are acting beneath your growth?

4.title: Servants, a Field
4.context: Planter and waterer are different jobs on the same crop. God made it grow is the sentence the whole picture hangs on, and it demotes both workers equally.
4.question: Whose watering of someone else's planting do you need to honor instead of envy?

4.title: One Foundation
4.context: Expert builder is a master craftsman's word. The foundation is declared unrepeatable: anyone who builds begins on Jesus Christ or builds on nothing.
4.question: What are you building that would not survive being measured against its foundation?

4.title: Revealed With Fire
4.context: The Day tests workmanship, not belonging: the builder whose work burns is himself saved, as through flames. Gold and straw are judged by endurance, not appearance.
4.question: Which of your works would you most fear to see tested by fire, and why?

4.title: God's Temple
4.context: The you is plural: the congregation together is the temple. Destroying it here is the work of division, and the warning is addressed to insiders, not enemies.
4.question: How have you seen a community damaged from inside, and what was your part in its care?

4.title: Become a Fool
4.context: The two quotations are Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11. Becoming a fool is the doorway to becoming wise, the same inversion as the cross itself.
4.question: What would becoming a fool for Christ look like in one concrete choice this week?

4.title: All Things Are Yours
4.context: The inheritance list includes the teachers themselves, plus life, death, present, and future. Ownership runs downward from Christ, never upward from a faction.
4.question: What do you already own in Christ that you keep striving to earn?

5.title: Stewards of the Mysteries
5.context: A steward manages what is not his. Found faithful is the whole job description: the finding is done by the owner, at his time.
5.question: What has been entrusted to you that you manage as if it were yours?

5.title: Judge Nothing Before the Time
5.context: Paul clears every human court including his own conscience, then sets one court date. Praise from God ends the verse, an outcome few of the Corinthians were picturing.
5.question: Whose verdict on you do you need to stop treating as final?

5.title: Not Beyond What Is Written
5.context: Applied to myself and Apollos is the method of the whole letter: Paul absorbs the correction into his own team first. Received is the question that ends all boasting.
5.question: What do you have that you did not receive, and how does the honest answer change your pride?

5.title: A Spectacle to the World
5.context: The procession image is a triumph parade read backwards: the apostles march last, as prisoners appointed for death, while the Corinthians imagine themselves already kings.
5.question: Where does your life look more like a spectacle than a throne, and what is God doing in it?

5.title: Not Many Fathers
5.context: Guardians were hired escorts for children; fathers are not hired. The imitation Paul requests is grounded in this one relationship and no other claim.
5.question: Who became a father or mother to you in the faith, and how do you imitate them?

5.title: A Rod, or Love
5.context: Timothy was already traveling as the letter went ahead of Paul. Talk and power is the test Paul promises to apply on arrival, to the arrogant first.
5.question: If Paul visited your life with this test, where would he find talk without power?

6.title: A Man Has His Father's Wife
6.context: The case is stated in the letter's own flat words and never named or narrated further. The church's pride, not only the man's act, is what Paul rebukes first.
6.question: What does your community tolerate proudly that it ought to grieve?

6.title: Hand This Man Over
6.context: The sentence carries its aim inside it: the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord. This letter does not report the outcome, and none is imported here.
6.question: How do you hold judgment and hope for someone together, the way this sentence does?

6.title: A Little Leaven
6.context: Leaven works invisibly and entirely, which is why one case is never one case. Christ our Passover lamb ties the cleansing to the feast Israel kept with unleavened bread.
6.question: What small tolerated thing in your life is quietly working through the whole batch?

6.title: The Letter Before This One
6.context: An earlier letter of Paul's is quoted only by its correction: it does not survive, and its words are never reconstructed. The boundary drawn is around the fellowship's table, not around the world.
6.question: Where do you draw the line between the world's company and the church's fellowship?

6.title: Expel the Wicked Man
6.context: The closing quotation is Deuteronomy's refrain, repeated after its case laws. Judgment inside and judgment outside are assigned to different judges, and Paul keeps them separate.
6.question: What judgment are you carrying that belongs to God and not to you?

7.title: Before the Saints
7.context: The future sets the present standard: people destined to judge the world and angels are taking trivial cases to courts that do not know God. Shame is Paul's stated aim in the argument.
7.question: When have you won a dispute and lost something worth more than the win?

7.title: Rather Be Wronged
7.context: Defeated already relocates the loss: the lawsuit itself, not its verdict. Being wronged and being cheated are treated as survivable; doing the wronging is not.
7.question: What wrong could you absorb rather than pass on, starting now?

7.title: Such Were Some of You
7.context: The catalog is quoted whole in the telling, and its answer is a past tense: washed, sanctified, justified. The list describes where the readers lived, not where they live now.
7.question: What is in your own were that you most need to remember was washed?

7.title: Everything Is Permissible
7.context: The slogans stand in Corinth's own quotation marks, answered by benefit and mastery. Food for the stomach pairs appetite with a body made for the Lord, not for use and disposal.
7.question: What permissible thing has quietly begun to master you?

7.title: Members of Christ
7.context: Resurrection is the body's future, stated mid-argument about the body's present. The Genesis words about one flesh are quoted to show union is never trivial.
7.question: How would you treat your body differently this week if you believed it will be raised?

7.title: Bought at a Price
7.context: Flight, not debate, is the command's shape. Temple language moves here from the congregation of chapter 3 to the single believer's body.
7.question: From what do you need to flee rather than negotiate, and what is your first step away?

8.title: The Matters You Wrote About
8.context: The chapter answers Corinth's own letter, and Paul labels his levels of authority as he goes: concession here, command later, judgment after that. The mutual-authority verse runs in both directions without qualification.
8.question: Where do you need to give in marriage, or withhold, more honestly than you have?

8.title: Better to Marry
8.context: Paul's preference for his own state never becomes a law for others. The alternative is stated without embarrassment: marriage is the good answer to burning.
8.question: What preference of yours do you need to stop treating as everyone else's rule?

8.title: Not I, but the Lord
8.context: The labels matter: the Lord's own command for the married, Paul's word for the cases Jesus never addressed. A mixed home is called holy ground, and the departing unbeliever releases rather than ruins.
8.question: If you are in a spiritually mixed home or close to one, what does peace look like there?

8.title: Remain as Called
8.context: Circumcision and slavery are the test cases of one rule for all the churches: the calling matters more than the circumstance. Freedom, when it can be had honorably, is to be taken.
8.question: What circumstance do you keep waiting to change before you will live your calling inside it?

8.title: The Time Is Short
8.context: No command from the Lord stands behind this section, and Paul says so; the judgment offered rests on the present crisis and the world's passing form. The as-if-not chain covers wives, tears, joy, and property in one sweep.
8.question: What do you hold as if it will last forever that this passage says is passing away?

8.title: Undivided Devotion
8.context: Concern is the chapter's measure: the same divided-interest account is kept for men and for women in matching terms. A widow's freedom closes the chapter, with Paul's judgment named as judgment.
8.question: What most divides your devotion right now, and what would undivided look like?

9.title: Knowledge Puffs Up
9.context: The slogan is Corinth's: we all have knowledge. Paul's counterweight is a building word, love builds up, against an inflation word. Being known by God outranks knowing.
9.question: Where is your knowledge inflating you in a place love should be building?

9.title: No God but One
9.context: The confession is complete and unconceded: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, with creation and existence assigned between them. The facts were never the dispute.
9.question: What true thing do you know that you are using in an unloving way?

9.title: A Weak Conscience
9.context: Weak here means still bound in conscience to the idol, not inferior in faith. Food itself is declared neutral in the same breath, so the danger is located in example, not diet.
9.question: Whose conscience is more tender than yours in a matter where you feel free?

9.title: Destroyed by Your Knowledge
9.context: The scene is a temple dining room: public, religious, and watched. For whom Christ died is the price tag attached to the brother the knowledge endangers.
9.question: Whose walk could your freedom quietly wreck this week, and what will you do instead?

9.title: Never Eat Meat Again
9.context: The vow is absolute and self-applied first: never again, over one brother's stumbling. Paul does not legislate the menu; he binds his own.
9.question: What freedom would you surrender permanently for one person's sake?

10.title: The Seal of My Apostleship
10.context: Four questions carry the credentials, and the congregation itself is the evidence: a seal authenticates a document the way Corinth authenticates Paul.
10.question: Who is the living evidence of your faithfulness, and have you told them?

10.title: Do Not Muzzle an Ox
10.context: Soldier, vineyard, flock, law, temple, and the Lord's own prescription line up behind one right. The ox text is Deuteronomy 25:4, read by Paul as written for us.
10.question: Whose gospel work do you benefit from, and how do you share materially in it?

10.title: Woe to Me
10.context: The rights are surrendered so completely that the reward is redefined as the surrender itself: preaching free of charge. Obligation, not preference, drives the preacher.
10.question: What obligation owns you in a way you have stopped resenting and started boasting in?

10.title: All Things to All People
10.context: Each form is adopted for the people inside it: Jew, those under the law, those without it, the weak. The law of Christ is named as the boundary he never crosses.
10.question: Whose world do you need to enter more fully to win them, and what is stopping you?

10.title: Run to Take the Prize
10.context: Corinth hosted the Isthmian games, second only to Olympia in Greece. The perishable crown was pine or celery wreath; the discipline described is a boxer's and a runner's, aimed at the preacher himself.
10.question: Where do you run aimlessly or swing at air, and what discipline would change it?

11.title: Struck Down in the Wilderness
11.context: All is the repeated word: all under the cloud, all through the sea, all baptized, all fed, and most struck down. The rock saying compresses Exodus and Numbers into one traveling provision.
11.question: What privilege do you lean on as if it were protection from falling?

11.title: Written Down as Warnings
11.context: Each example carries its toll, and the twenty-three thousand of Numbers 25 stands as written in Paul's count. Fulfillment of the ages frames the readers as the generation the warnings were saved for.
11.question: Which of these five examples is aimed closest to your own weak point?

11.title: An Escape
11.context: The promise measures temptation by what is common to man and caps it by God's faithfulness. The escape makes standing possible; it does not promise the temptation will not come.
11.question: What escape has God already provided in a temptation you keep calling unbeatable?

11.title: The Cup and the Table
11.context: Participation is the argument's key word: a shared cup and loaf make one body, and altars bind their eaters. The idol is nothing; the demons behind the sacrifices are not.
11.question: What two tables are you trying to sit at, and which one keeps losing?

11.title: The Other One's Conscience
11.context: The slogan appears for the last time, fully answered. Market and dinner table are free until another's conscience speaks, at which point love governs what knowledge permits.
11.question: When did you last surrender a right for a conscience that was not your own?

11.title: Do It All to the Glory of God
11.context: Eating and drinking are named first in the all: the ordinary is the arena. Imitate me closes the section by pointing at Christ through Paul, never at Paul alone.
11.question: What ordinary act of yours this week most needs to be done to God's glory on purpose?

12.title: Maintaining the Traditions
12.context: The praise is real and limited to remembrance and tradition kept. It is the last praise in this part of the letter; the following instructions begin with its absence.
12.question: What tradition handed to you are you keeping well, and who handed it to you?

12.title: The Head of Every Man
12.context: This passage is carried as the letter gives it, in Paul's order, because churches have read its practice differently across centuries. The headship chain is stated before any practice is drawn from it.
12.question: How do you read a passage faithfully when faithful people around you apply it differently?

12.title: In the Lord, Not Independent
12.context: Creation order is argued, and then mutual dependence is stated inside the same argument: woman from man, man born of woman, everything from God. Both halves are the letter's.
12.question: Where do you need to hold both halves of a teaching instead of only the half that suits you?

12.title: Judge for Yourselves
12.context: Custom, nature, and the practice of all the churches close the section. Long hair given as a covering is nature's exhibit in the argument as Paul makes it.
12.question: What practice in your church rests on custom, and how do you hold it with grace toward others?

12.title: More Harm Than Good
12.context: In part I believe it measures the report: the divisions were credible because the evidence kept arriving. Differences showing who is approved is a hard word, carried as written.
12.question: What report about your community would you believe in part, because you have seen the signs?

12.title: One Remains Hungry
12.context: The meal behind the Supper was a real supper in a house church, eaten at different hours by people of different means. Going ahead without sharing is the abuse in one phrase.
12.question: Who goes hungry, literally or otherwise, at the edges of your fellowship while you feast?

12.title: On the Night He Was Betrayed
12.context: Received and passed on is the same chain as the creed of chapter 15. This is the earliest written account of the Supper's words, set down before any Gospel, and it dates the gift to the betrayal night itself.
12.question: What do you proclaim, and to whom, every time you eat this bread and drink this cup?

12.title: Examine Himself
12.context: The remedy for an abused table is examination before eating, and the discipline described is called the Lord's, aimed at not being condemned with the world. Wait for one another is the practical sum.
12.question: What examination do you need to make before the next time you come to the table?

13.title: Jesus Is Lord
13.context: The test of every spirit is a confession, not an experience: no Spirit-speaker curses Jesus, and no one confesses him Lord except by the Spirit. Mute idols stand behind the readers as the contrast.
13.question: What confession do you need to make the test of the voices you listen to?

13.title: For the Common Good
13.context: Same Spirit, same Lord, same God is said three ways over three kinds of variety. The catalogue ends with one distributor apportioning as he determines, not as the gifted decide.
13.question: Which gift in your church do you undervalue because it is not yours?

13.title: One Body
13.context: Baptized into one body names the entrance; given one Spirit to drink names the ongoing life. Jew and Greek, slave and free are Corinth's own ranks, leveled in one verse.
13.question: Where do you still rank people inside a body where this verse leveled them?

13.title: The Foot and the Ear
13.context: The members' speeches are imagined by Paul and refuted by anatomy. Arranged according to his design answers the inferiority half of the body's argument.
13.question: Which part of the body do you secretly believe you are, and which part do you envy?

13.title: I Do Not Need You
13.context: The superiority half is answered with honor redistributed downward. Mutual concern is the design's stated purpose, and suffering and rejoicing are both made contagious.
13.question: Whose suffering in your church have you not yet let become your own?

13.title: Eagerly Desire the Greater Gifts
13.context: The appointment order is God's; the closing questions expect no for an answer. The most excellent way is announced as a showing, and chapter 13 is the exhibit.
13.question: What greater gift should you be desiring, for the body's sake rather than your own?

14.title: A Ringing Gong
14.context: Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, and total sacrifice are each weighed without love. The verdicts descend: noise, nothing, no gain.
14.question: Which of your best gifts is likeliest to be running without love right now?

14.title: Love Is Patient
14.context: Every line describes conduct toward people, and nearly every line answers a Corinthian behavior named earlier in the letter: boasting, rudeness, account-keeping, self-seeking.
14.question: Which line of this portrait is your clearest conviction, and what would obeying it look like tomorrow?

14.title: Love Never Fails
14.context: Cease, restrained, and dismissed are the gifts' verbs; never fails is love's. The partial is not called false, only temporary, like everything that belongs to this age of the story.
14.question: What are you treating as permanent that this chapter says will pass away?

14.title: Face to Face
14.context: The ancient mirror was polished metal, giving a dim reflection by design. Fully known precedes knowing fully: God's knowledge of us is the ground of ours of him.
14.question: How does being fully known by God change the way you pray about what you only know in part?

14.title: The Greatest of These
14.context: Faith, hope, and love remain when the gifts are gone, and love is ranked above the two no one expected to see outranked. The chapter ends the gifts debate by enlarging it.
14.question: Of faith, hope, and love, which is weakest in you this season, and what would feed it?

15.title: Especially Prophecy
15.context: Pursue love is the first command, and it governs the desiring that follows. Edification, encouragement, and comfort define prophecy's speech to men.
15.question: Do your words in church mostly edify, encourage, and comfort, or do they do something else?

15.title: Speaking Into the Air
15.context: Flute, harp, and trumpet argue that sound without distinction is noise in worship as in war. Many languages have meaning; an unknown one makes foreigners of friends.
15.question: When has your speech about God been ten thousand words where five coherent ones were needed?

15.title: Pray With My Mind
15.context: Spirit and mind are set side by side in prayer and song, not against each other. The uninstructed man's Amen is treated as a real stake in how the church prays aloud.
15.question: Where does your prayer life run on spirit without mind, or mind without spirit?

15.title: God Is Truly Among You
15.context: The Law quotation is Isaiah 28:11-12, a sign that hardened rather than helped. Two visitors measure the assembly: one leaves calling it madness, one falls facedown.
15.question: What would a visitor conclude about God from your church's ordinary Sunday?

15.title: In a Proper and Orderly Manner
15.context: Two or three, in turn, with weighing: the rules are quotas of courtesy grounded in God's own character. Disorder is never blamed on the Spirit in this chapter.
15.question: What disorder in your shared life with God's people needs a courteous rule rather than more enthusiasm?

15.title: As in All the Churches
15.context: These verses stand in every surviving copy of the letter, in the place the letter gives them, and churches have applied them differently across the centuries; the telling carries them as written and takes no side the text does not. Paul claims the Lord's command for the instruction and Corinth's originality is denied.
15.question: How do you obey a command whose application your church reads differently from another faithful church?

15.title: Do Not Forbid
15.context: Both halves are commands: eager for prophecy, and no forbidding of tongues. The order that governs the chapter is a manner, not a muzzle.
15.question: Which half of this closing command is harder for you, and why?

16.title: Hold Firmly
16.context: Received, stand firm, and saved all hang on holding firmly. The reminder assumes the gospel is already known; what is failing is not information but grip.
16.question: What part of the gospel you received do you most need to tighten your grip on?

16.title: He Appeared to Cephas
16.context: Received and passed on marks this as creed, older than the letter: died, buried, raised, appeared, each according to the Scriptures or to named witnesses. Five hundred at once, most still living when Paul wrote, could be asked.
16.question: Which witness in this list do you find most compelling, and why that one?

16.title: Least of the Apostles
16.context: The persecutor's shame and the laborer's boast are held in one verse and assigned to grace twice. Whether I or they dissolves even apostolic rivalry into one preached message.
16.question: What in your past do you call disqualifying that grace has already answered?

16.title: If Christ Has Not Been Raised
16.context: The chain is deliberately merciless: preaching worthless, faith futile, witnesses false, sins unforgiven, the dead perished, the living pitied. Paul lets the denial cost everything before he answers it.
16.question: What would you actually lose if the resurrection were not true, and do you live as if you know it?

16.title: Firstfruits
16.context: Firstfruits is a harvest pledge, not a private exception: what happened to Christ is the first sheaf of a crop. The end sequence is carried as written, ending with God all in all.
16.question: Whose resurrection do you most look forward to besides your own, and what will you say first?

16.title: Baptized for the Dead
16.context: This single verse is carried unexpanded, the way the letter leaves it: Paul cites a practice as an argument for resurrection without explaining or commending it. His own daily danger is the paired exhibit.
16.question: What do you risk daily, small or large, that only makes sense if the dead are raised?

16.title: Sober Up
16.context: The proverb is a line from the Greek playwright Menander, quoted as common wisdom. Ignorant of God, from the apostle to his own converts, is the section's last diagnosis.
16.question: Whose company is quietly corrupting your character, and what distance do you owe the truth?

17.title: What You Sow
17.context: The objector's two questions are quoted before they are answered. A seed's death and transformation is the farm's everyday miracle, and the body it receives is assigned, not evolved from the seed's effort.
17.question: What has God grown in your life from something that first had to die?

17.title: Star Differs From Star
17.context: Flesh and splendor are both catalogued in kinds. A God who fits every creature and every star with its own body and degree of glory is not short of designs for the dead.
17.question: Where do you compare your splendor with another's instead of receiving your own?

17.title: Raised Imperishable
17.context: Four pairs run perishable to imperishable, dishonor to glory, weakness to power, natural to spiritual. The Genesis quotation is 2:7, applied to the first Adam to define the last.
17.question: Which pair in this drumbeat speaks most directly to your own body's story?

17.title: We Will All Be Changed
17.context: Mystery names a disclosed secret, not a hidden one. Twinkling of an eye is Paul's measure of the change, and the trumpet is the last one: no signal follows it.
17.question: What about your present body do you most need to hear will be changed rather than merely ended?

17.title: Swallowed Up in Victory
17.context: The saying is Isaiah 25:8, and the taunt is Hosea 13:14 turned into a victory cry. Sin and law are named as the sting and its power, so the thanksgiving that follows is precise, not general.
17.question: What would you say to death, in this chapter's words, at the grave of someone you love?

17.title: Not in Vain
17.context: The most cosmic chapter in the letter closes with ordinary labor blessed. Steadfast and immovable describe people whose work outlasts them because the Lord is raised.
17.question: What work of yours feels vain right now, and how does this verse reframe it?

18.title: On the First Day of Every Week
18.context: The collection is for the saints in Jerusalem, organized weekly and privately so no pressure collection is needed at Paul's arrival. Galatia had the same directions; Corinth is not an exception.
18.question: What generosity of yours would grow if it became weekly, small, and planned?

18.title: I Will Stay in Ephesus
18.context: The letter's writing city is named only here, near its end. A great door and many opponents are reported in one breath, as if opposition were a normal feature of an open door.
18.question: Where is your open door right now, and who are its opponents?

18.title: Apollos Will Go When
18.context: Timothy is to be protected from contempt and sent on in peace. Apollos, urged strongly, declines for now: the letter respects his timing and reports it without frustration.
18.question: Whose timing have you needed to respect instead of overruling, and how did it go?

18.title: Do Everything in Love
18.context: Five commands stand like a watchword, and love governs the set. Stephanas's household, the delegation that carried Corinth's questions, is honored for self-devoted service, not for status.
18.question: Which of the five commands is yours to obey first this week?

18.title: The Church at Their House
18.context: Aquila and Prisca are the tentmakers of Acts 18, Corinth's own first hosts, greeting their old church from Ephesus with a congregation in their house. Asia's churches widen the circle beyond one city.
18.question: Whose house, including possibly yours, has become a place where the church gathers or is strengthened?

18.title: My Own Hand
18.context: The own-hand greeting authenticates the letter as in the Thessalonian letters. The curse and the love stand in the same closing: Come, O Lord is Aramaic maranatha, kept by the earliest churches in its original tongue.
18.question: What would the mark of your own hand say at the end of your hardest letter?
